doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: How he met Steve Allen and the Regis Philbin Show
summary: Allen was a fan; Gibbs became bandleader and second banana on the Regis Philbin Show with a sextet.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: In fact that band, that size band is what I used when I was conducting with Steve. The sextet. With the clarinet, guitar and vibes, and piano, bass and drums.
How did you get to know him?

Well I got to know him, he was a fan of mine. [pause for refreshment] That’s right keep bringing ‘em in. Stop putting all that vodka in this. I quit drinking years ago. I thank you very much. He was a fan of mine. He used to come, in New York, when I played Birdland. He’d come in all the time to hear me. And when I moved out to California he’d come in to see me playing all the time. And I moved back to New York for almost a year and I got called, he was doing a television show and I got called — he quit the show by the way, he quit the show. He had some kind of thing with Westinghouse, boom he quit. And they booked this young kid in, Regis Philbin. That he was going to start the next week. And the people who produced “The Steve Allen Show” liked when I appeared as a guest with Steve. They liked my dumb sense of humor and what I did, and they knew I can play, and they didn’t care if I knew how to conduct or anything, they called me and asked me if I would audition, not playing, I’d be the second banana, you know, as a band leader, with what kind of rapport I’d have with Regis. And two other guys were Barney, I mean Bobby Troup — I didn’t know this — and Ray Anthony, both up for the job. But they liked what I had to say you know. And then they wanted to give me a nine piece band. They said — wait, you got the job, a nine piece band, that’s what Steve had. I said no, I don’t want the job with nine pieces. First of all we were on at night opposite Les Crane at that time who had Elliott Lawrence and sixteen pieces, and Johnny Carson, who had Doc Severinsen. I said if we have nine pieces are we going to try to sound like sixteen? I said either give me sixteen or give me a sextet. And we weren’t in competition with anybody. They said, “Can you make it work with six?” I said, “I’ll make it work, no problem.” And so the Regis Philbin Show, and by the way he’s one of the nicest people living. I taped one of these shows about a month ago which will be shown sometime in January. I’m not sure when this is going to be shown, but sometime in January it will be shown. And we got along great. In fact, I was the second banana, Regis wasn’t into jazz at all. He really didn’t know much about jazz, and we’d have Count — and they weren’t fair to Regis, really. Because all the guests that were booked for the first ten weeks probably were Steve Allen’s guests that were booked a long time ago. And Regis, that’s not his bag. Jazz people are not his bag. We’d have Sarah Vaughan, Count Basie, we had all the heavyweight players. And we had Count Basie on. I remember when we had Count Basie. Count Basie is the worst interview in the world. He could yes and no you to death. You know if you were sitting here with me and you asked me a question and I’d say, “yes” “no.” You’d have a nervous breakdown after a while. So Regis would ask him

a question, “yes,” “no,” he asked him. Finally I said, “Regis, I want to ask Basie a question.” He said, “Go ahead, Terry.” I went down and said, “Basie, when we played in Detroit that time, remember that scene with Pee Wee Marquette? Tell Regis.” He had to tell the story now. So every time we had a jazz musician — Stan Getz, every time he interviewed, I had to be down there with him. He was really great. That wasn’t his bag. I used to put him on all the time. He always thought that we were putting him on because we were jazz players. But we really loved him. He loved the band and he always praised the band.
